title: Event home
text:
Purpose
The increasing availability of data sources, alternative to traditional data collection, has opened new opportunities for improving the compilation of consumer price statistics. Amongst these sources, scanner data, web scraped, and administrative data are the more prominent. Many National Statistical Offices (NSOs) are actively exploring the use of these new sources of data to enhance price measurement, expand product coverage, and improve timeliness and quality of Consumer Price Indices (CPI).
In response to this growing interest, the UN Task Team on Scanner Data has developed a rich set of methodological materials, guidelines, and practical tools, made available through its public wiki and related repositories. These resources provide a solid foundation for NSOs at different stages of adoption.
Building on this work, the UN Regional Hub for Big Data in Brazil proposes to jointly organize, with the UN Task Team on Scanner Data, a regional workshop aimed at supporting NSOs in Latin America and the Caribbean in their practical use of the new data sources for CPI compilation with a focus on scanner data use.

title: Pre-requisites for synchronous and asynchronous coding activities
text:
The idea
For synchronous and asynchronous coding activities we suggest users to leverage an online service to run Python and R code.
The main environment suggested is Google colab, which has a generous free tier at the moment of writing (June 2026).
You can use an existing Google account to access it, or create a new one dedicated to the course activities. Just make sure to get access to it before the start of the course to avoid any delay.
Of course you are free to use another online platform of your choice or your own computer. However, since the time dedicated to coding activities is quite limited, trainers may not be able to provide assistence on environments other than Colab in case of issues. Therefore, in case you choose to use a different environment you are expected to be able to independetly manage it.


To-Do list

Get access to a Google account (pre-existing or new one) before the start of the course
Watch two brief introductory videos on Colab: Introduction to Google Colab (3 mins) and Google Colab features you may have missed (5 mins)
Experiment with a Google Colab notebook to get familiar with the environment

title: Event agenda
text:
The workshop is proposed as a five-day virtual event, combining synchronous and asynchronous activities, to balance live interaction with flexibility for participants.

Synchronous sessions are proposed for Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, from 10:00 to 12:00 (Brasília time, GMT-3). These sessions would focus on conceptual discussions, methodological guidance, live demonstrations, and interactive exchanges with the Task Team.
Asynchronous activities are proposed for Tuesday and Thursday, allowing participants to engage with selected materials, exercises, or practical tasks at their own pace. These activities would build on the content of the synchronous sessions and reinforce key concepts and tools

title: Data preparation, cleaning, and classification
text:
Overview of the data
The data comes in 4 separate parts:

A definition of weeks
A definition of stores
The unique product (i.e. UPC) files per category
The sales (i.e. movement) files, again per category. This is total turnover and quantities sold per UPC per week.

As NSOs typically get a week’s file that will include all this information (and things like week definitions would typically be defined as time goes on), we should join these 4 datasets into one. NSOs typically also receive all the data in one batch (irrespective of the category of the products, indeed the assigning of product the right category is classification). Thus for demonstration purposes, we’ll join two product categories (movements and UPC files) into one big file.

To work with the data, we can do a few things: - convert the dates into actual datetime objects to make manipulation easy - create a custom variable that tells us what reference period the weekly file belongs to (say "1996-01") as we measure the CPI on a monthly basis - evaluate if a week falls cleanly within the month (does it start at the end of one month and end in the beginning of the next one) and if it does fall within the month, what week number is it?2


Show the code
# First off, cast the START and END columns to datetime
df['START'] = pd.to_datetime(df['START'], format='%m/%d/%y')
df['END'] = pd.to_datetime(df['END'], format='%m/%d/%y')

# Now we can extract the reference period (month) and determine if the week is fully in the month
df['REF_PERIOD'] = df['START'].dt.strftime('%Y-%m')

# Now we can determine if the week is fully in the month by checking if the month of the start and end dates are the same
df['WEEK_FULLY_IN_MONTH'] = np.where(
        df['START'].dt.month == df['END'].dt.month, 
        True, 
        np.nan
    )

valid_weeks = df['WEEK_FULLY_IN_MONTH'].notna()
df['WEEK_OF_MONTH'] = (
        valid_weeks
        .groupby(df['REF_PERIOD'])
        .cumsum()
        .where(valid_weeks, np.nan)
    )

show(df.head(50))

title: Data preparation, cleaning, and classification
text:
Footnotes


We need to assign prices/quanitities to the months they happen in, however if we receive data that stradles two months, there may not be a clean way to separate it out. We we can start with the first clean week. Furthermore, as we have a deadline to publish the CPI (typically early in the month following the one we are measuring), it is sometimes challenging to include all the weekly data. See Chapter 3 of the Eurostat Multilateral guide for more on aggregation across time.↩︎
